title: Hurwitz's Theorem: Statement, Strategy, and Historical Note
content: The docstring explains the theorem's structure: an n-square identity exists only for n ∈ {1,2,4,8}, and these correspond to the four normed division algebras ℝ, ℂ, ℍ, 𝕆. The proof approach is split: existence direction (if n ∈ {1,2,4,8} then identity exists) is fully proved for n=1,2,4 with n=8 axiomatized; non-existence direction (only if) requires Clifford algebras. Hurwitz's personal note: Hamilton searched for 15 years for a 3-dimensional 'triplet' algebra — Hurwitz's theorem proves this search was futile.
mathContext: An n-square identity: bilinear maps $B_1, \ldots, B_n : \mathbb{R}^n \times \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ such that $(\sum_i x_i^2)(\sum_i y_i^2) = \sum_i B_i(x,y)^2$. Equivalent to: a normed composition algebra of dimension $n$ over $\mathbb{R}$. The complete list is $\{1,2,4,8\}$ — ℝ, ℂ, ℍ, 𝕆.

title: NSquareIdentity: The Formal Structure for Bilinear Norm Identities
content: NSquareIdentity (n : ℕ) is a Lean structure capturing the algebraic content of an n-square identity: a bilinear map `mul : (Fin n → ℝ) → (Fin n → ℝ) → (Fin n → ℝ)` satisfying left/right additivity, left/right scalar compatibility, and the key `norm_mul` property that ‖a‖²·‖b‖² = ‖mul a b‖². The four field-law-like axioms (add_left, add_right, smul_left, smul_right) make `mul` a bilinear map, while `norm_mul` is the composition identity. Each known algebra (ℝ, ℂ, ℍ, 𝕆) gives one NSquareIdentity instance.
mathContext: Structure fields: $(1)$ `add_left`: $B(a+b, c) = B(a,c) + B(b,c)$ (left additivity). $(2)$ `add_right`: $B(a, b+c) = B(a,b) + B(a,c)$. $(3)$ `smul_left`: $B(r \cdot a, b) = r \cdot B(a,b)$. $(4)$ `smul_right`: $B(a, r \cdot b) = r \cdot B(a,b)$. $(5)$ `norm_mul`: $\|a\|^2 \cdot \|b\|^2 = \|B(a,b)\|^2$. Together $(1)$-$(4)$ make $B$ bilinear, and $(5)$ makes it a composition.

title: 2-Square Identity: Brahmagupta-Fibonacci via Complex Multiplication
content: twoMul (a b : Fin 2 → ℝ) defines (a₀,a₁)×(b₀,b₁) = (a₀b₀-a₁b₁, a₀b₁+a₁b₀), which is precisely complex number multiplication. two_square_identity proves ‖a‖²·‖b‖² = ‖twoMul a b‖² by ring. The twoSquareIdentity structure wraps this as an NSquareIdentity 2 — all bilinearity fields are proved by fin_cases on the two indices and ring. The identity itself is: (x₁²+x₂²)(y₁²+y₂²) = (x₁y₁-x₂y₂)²+(x₁y₂+x₂y₁)², known since Brahmagupta (628 CE) and rediscovered by Fibonacci (1202).
mathContext: Brahmagupta-Fibonacci identity: $(x_1^2 + x_2^2)(y_1^2 + y_2^2) = (x_1y_1 - x_2y_2)^2 + (x_1y_2 + x_2y_1)^2$. Proof by ring arithmetic. This is norm multiplicativity of $\mathbb{C}$: $|z|^2 = x_1^2 + x_2^2$ for $z = x_1 + ix_2$, and $|zw|^2 = |z|^2|w|^2$.

title: 4-Square Identity: Euler's Identity via Quaternion Multiplication
content: fourMul defines quaternion multiplication in coordinates: (a₀,a₁,a₂,a₃)×(b₀,b₁,b₂,b₃) gives the four Hamilton product components. four_square_identity proves ‖a‖²·‖b‖² = ‖fourMul a b‖² using simp + ring with increased maxHeartbeats (800000) for the algebraic expansion. The identity was discovered by Euler (1748) long before Hamilton discovered quaternions (1843) — Euler saw it as a number-theoretic curiosity, not knowing its algebraic source. The maxHeartbeats setting is needed because the ring tactic must expand a degree-4 polynomial identity in 8 variables.
mathContext: Euler's 4-square identity: $(\sum_{i=1}^4 a_i^2)(\sum_{i=1}^4 b_i^2) = \sum_{i=1}^4 c_i^2$ where the $c_i$ are the quaternion product components. Quaternion norm multiplicativity: $|q_1 q_2|^2 = |q_1|^2 |q_2|^2$. In coordinates: if $q = a_0 + a_1 i + a_2 j + a_3 k$, then $|q|^2 = a_0^2 + a_1^2 + a_2^2 + a_3^2$.

title: Quaternion Connection and 8-Square (Octonion) Identity
content: Part 5 connects to Mathlib's quaternion library: `quaternion_norm_mul` proves $|q_1 q_2|^2 = |q_1|^2 |q_2|^2$ via `Quaternion.normSq.map_mul`, providing an alternative proof of the 4-square identity using Mathlib's existing infrastructure. Part 6 handles the 8-square identity from octonion multiplication. The octonionic norm identity $|o_1 o_2| = |o_1| |o_2|$ gives an 8-square identity with each component being a sum of 8 signed products. The Cayley-Dickson doubling construction builds 𝕆 from ℍ via $(p,q)(r,s) = (pr - \bar{s}q, sp + q\bar{r})$ where $p,q,r,s \in \mathbb{H}$. The 8-square identity was first discovered by C.F. Degen in 1818, predating Cayley's octonions by 25 years.
mathContext: Quaternion norm multiplicativity: $|q_1 q_2|^2 = |q_1|^2 |q_2|^2$ for $q_1, q_2 \in \mathbb{H}$. Cayley-Dickson doubling: $\mathbb{O} = \mathbb{H} \oplus \mathbb{H}$ with $(p,q)(r,s) = (pr - \bar{s}q, sp + q\bar{r})$. Degen's 8-square identity (1818): $(\sum_{i=1}^8 x_i^2)(\sum_{i=1}^8 y_i^2) = \sum_{i=1}^8 z_i^2$ where each $z_i$ is bilinear in $x,y$.

title: Inner Product and 3D Geometry Infrastructure for Impossibility Proof
content: The largest section (548 lines) builds the supporting machinery for proving no 3-square identity exists. Defines `innerProd` on `Fin 3 → ℝ`, `stdBasis`, and `normSq` in terms of componentwise sums. Key lemmas include: (1) `orthogonality_constraint` — bilinearity of an NSquareIdentity forces orthogonal inputs to produce orthogonal outputs; (2) `inner_expansion_three` — any vector in ℝ³ expands as a linear combination of three orthonormal vectors; (3) `unit_ortho_two_eq_pm_third` — a unit vector orthogonal to two of three orthonormal basis vectors must equal ±(the third). These lemmas encode the finite-dimensional geometry that makes ℝ³ too small to support a normed composition algebra. The proof is essentially linear algebra: bilinearity forces images of basis vectors to be orthonormal, but ℝ³ has only 3 mutually orthogonal directions.
mathContext: Key geometric fact: in $\mathbb{R}^3$, any three mutually orthogonal unit vectors form a basis. If $B : \mathbb{R}^3 \times \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}^3$ is bilinear with $\|B(x,y)\|^2 = \|x\|^2 \|y\|^2$, then the 9 vectors $B(e_i, e_j)$ must all be unit vectors ($\|B(e_i,e_j)\| = 1$) and the columns $\{B(e_1,e_j), B(e_2,e_j), B(e_3,e_j)\}$ must be orthonormal. But ℝ³ only has room for 3 mutually orthogonal directions, creating an overdetermined system.

title: No 3-Square Identity: Overdetermined Orthonormality Contradiction
content: no_three_square_identity_proof (nsi : NSquareIdentity 3) : False is the core impossibility. Strategy: if a 3-square identity exists, the images mᵢⱼ = nsi.mul(eᵢ, eⱼ) of standard basis pairs form unit vectors in ℝ³ by norm_mul. The orthogonality_constraint lemmas show that eᵢ ⊥ eⱼ implies nsi.mul(eᵢ,v) ⊥ nsi.mul(eⱼ,v) for all v. This forces too many mutually orthogonal unit vectors into ℝ³, which can only have 3. The Gram-Schmidt decomposition and dimensional argument yield a contradiction via the geometric lemmas in Part 7 (inner_expansion_three, unit_ortho_two_eq_pm_third, inner_bilinear_expansion).
mathContext: Key step: if $e_1, e_2, e_3$ are orthonormal in $\mathbb{R}^3$ and $B$ is a bilinear composition, then $B(e_1, e_1), B(e_2, e_1), B(e_3, e_1)$ must be orthonormal (column 1 orthonormality). Similarly for other columns. This gives $\geq 9$ unit vectors in $\mathbb{R}^3$, all pairwise orthogonal — impossible since $\mathbb{R}^3$ has dimension 3. Formally: the linear span argument via `inner_bilinear_expansion` and `unit_ortho_two_eq_pm_third` derives a non-zero vector equal to zero, a contradiction.

title: Hurwitz's Theorem: Assembly of Existence and Non-Existence
content: admissibleDimensions : Set ℕ = {1,2,4,8} defines the four valid dimensions. identities_exist_for_admissible proves all four exist by case analysis: each of the four NSquareIdentity instances (oneSquareIdentity, twoSquareIdentity, fourSquareIdentity, eightSquareIdentity) is returned for the corresponding case. The axiom hurwitz_only_if captures the non-existence direction. hurwitz_theorem combines these into the biconditional: NSquareIdentity n is nonempty ↔ n ∈ admissibleDimensions. The four-line proof — constructor, then each direction by one application — demonstrates how all prior work assembles cleanly.
mathContext: $\exists B : \text{NSquareIdentity}\,n \iff n \in \{1,2,4,8\}$. The $\Rightarrow$ direction uses `hurwitz_only_if` (the axiom). The $\Leftarrow$ direction uses `identities_exist_for_admissible` (the constructive proof). The overall structure is `Iff.intro (fun ⟨nsi⟩ => hurwitz_only_if n hn nsi) (identities_exist_for_admissible n)`.

title: The Four Normed Division Algebras: Properties and Significance
content: DivisionAlgebra is an inductive type with four constructors: reals (ℝ, dim 1), complex (ℂ, dim 2), quaternions (ℍ, dim 4), octonions (𝕆, dim 8). division_algebra_identity proves each has dimension in admissibleDimensions by cases on the constructor. The comment block explains the four algebras' properties — losing ordering (ℝ→ℂ), commutativity (ℂ→ℍ), and associativity (ℍ→𝕆) — and connections to physics (quantum mechanics, 3D rotations, string theory) and topology (parallelizable spheres S⁰, S¹, S³, S⁷).
mathContext: Each step loses a property: $\mathbb{R}$ (ordered, complete) $\to$ $\mathbb{C}$ (lose ordering) $\to$ $\mathbb{H}$ (lose commutativity) $\to$ $\mathbb{O}$ (lose associativity). Beyond $\mathbb{O}$, the Cayley-Dickson construction gives sedenions (16-dim) which have zero divisors, destroying division. Topological equivalent: only $S^0, S^1, S^3, S^7$ are parallelizable — corresponding to $n-1$ for $n \in \{1,2,4,8\}$ (Adams's theorem, 1962, using K-theory).
